name: Central Intelligence Agency

summary.text: The Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) is the main foreign intelligence agency of the U.S. government. Declassified records show it helped plan and execute the 1953 coup that overthrew Iranian Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddeq. The Senate Church Committee reported in 1976 that the CIA had covert relationships with about 50 American journalists or media employees. In 1999 the CIA set up In-Q-Tel, an independent not-for-profit strategic investment firm.

facts.claim: The Senate Church Committee's 1976 final report found that, until February 1976, the CIA maintained covert relationships with about 50 American journalists or employees of U.S. media organizations. These were part of a network of several hundred foreign individuals who provided intelligence to the CIA and at times tried to influence foreign opinion through covert propaganda.

sources.publisher: U.S. Senate Select Committee to Study Governmental Operations with Respect to Intelligence Activities
sources.title: Final Report, Book I: Foreign and Military Intelligence

facts.claim: In 1953 the CIA, together with British intelligence (SIS), planned and executed Operation TPAJAX, which overthrew Iranian Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddeq on August 19, 1953, two years after Iran nationalized the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company. Coup organizers paid bands of demonstrators in Tehran.

facts.claim: The Independent Counsel for Iran/Contra Matters charged three CIA officers. Alan D. Fiers Jr., chief of the Central American Task Force, pleaded guilty in July 1991 to two misdemeanor counts of withholding information from Congress about covert aid to the Nicaraguan contras and was sentenced on January 31, 1992 to one year of probation and 100 hours of community service. Clair E. George, deputy director for operations, was indicted on September 6, 1991 and, after a mistrial, was found guilty on December 9, 1992 of two felony counts of false statements and perjury before Congress.
facts.quote: found guilty December 9, 1992, of two felony charges of false statements and perjury before Congress

facts.claim: Duane R. Clarridge, a former CIA division chief, was indicted on November 26, 1991 on seven counts of perjury and false statements about a secret November 1985 shipment of U.S. HAWK missiles to Iran. On December 24, 1992 President Bush pardoned Clarridge before his trial, Clair George before sentencing and Alan Fiers after sentencing, together with Caspar Weinberger, Elliott Abrams and Robert McFarlane.
facts.quote: On December 24, 1992, President Bush pardoned Caspar W. Weinberger, Duane R. Clarridge, Clair E. George, Elliott Abrams, Alan D. Fiers, Jr., and Robert C. McFarlane.

facts.claim: The Senate Foreign Relations Committee report on BCCI (December 1992) recorded the CIA's testimony, through Acting Director Richard Kerr, that the agency had not been involved with or had knowledge of any use of BCCI for the sale of arms to Iran or the diversion of funds to the Nicaraguan contras; the report itself stated that BCCI was used by key Iran/Contra figures to finance arms shipments to Iran and that in some cases the extent of U.S. official involvement could not be determined.
facts.quote: had not been involved with or had knowledge of any use of BCCI for the same of arms to Iran or the diversion of funds for the Nicaraguan Contras

facts.claim: On June 25, 2025, CIA Director John Ratcliffe issued a statement that a body of credible intelligence indicated Iran's nuclear program had been severely damaged by the recent targeted strikes, citing new intelligence from a historically reliable and accurate source/method that several key Iranian nuclear facilities were destroyed and would have to be rebuilt over the course of years. The statement followed press reports of a Defense Intelligence Agency initial assessment that the strikes had set the program back by months; CNN noted it was unclear whether the statement was an official agency assessment or the Director's view.
facts.quote: CIA can confirm that a body of credible intelligence indicates Iran's Nuclear Program has been severely damaged by the recent, targeted strikes.

connections.claim: After Iran nationalized the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company (BP's predecessor) in 1951, the CIA and British intelligence organized the August 1953 coup that removed Prime Minister Mosaddeq. Under a 1954 agreement with the post-coup government, AIOC took a 40% interest in the consortium operating Iran's oil industry.

sources.title: CIA Confirms Role in 1953 Iran Coup

connections.toName: Bank of Credit and Commerce International
connections.claim: The Senate Foreign Relations Committee report by Senators Kerry and Brown (December 1992) found that, after the CIA knew BCCI was as an institution a fundamentally corrupt criminal enterprise, it continued to use both BCCI and First American, BCCI's secretly held U.S. subsidiary, for CIA operations. The CIA's witness, Kerr, acknowledged the CIA had used BCCI for certain intelligence-gathering operations and called the use limited and routine; former First American president Robert Altman testified the CIA made extensive use of First American; and former Customs Commissioner William von Raab said Customs agents had found several BCCI accounts actually held by the CIA.
connections.quote: After the CIA knew that BCCI was as an institution a fundamentally corrupt criminal enterprise, it continued to use both BCCI and First American, BCCI's secretly held U.S. subsidiary, for CIA operations.

openQuestions: Iran-Contra and 2025 items appended 2026-10-09. The CIA-officer prosecution details come from the Walsh Summary of Prosecutions and Part VI excerpts; Clarridge's indictment concerned the November 1985 HAWK shipment to Iran, per Chapter 18. The Tower Commission's finding that NSC staff rather than the CIA directed the Iran deals appears in Time's 1987 summary but was not captured from the report text itself, so it is not recorded as a fact.
